strengths: Significance: A single model supporting optional geometric priors, geometric prediction, surface normals, and Gaussian-based rendering would be practically useful. The manuscript demonstrates substantially broader functionality than the underlying VGGT model.

Empirical evidence: The reported novel-view synthesis gains are substantial across sparse and dense inputs. In Table 4, image-only WorldMirror improves RealEstate10K PSNR over AnySplat from 17.62 to 20.62 with two views and from 19.96 to 25.14 with 32 views. Table 3 also reports strong surface-normal results, including ScanNet mean angular error of 13.8 versus 16.0 for StableNormal.

Originality: The contribution is primarily a useful integration of prior conditioning and additional prediction tasks. Modality-specific tokenization is straightforward, and Table 5 provides evidence that compact camera tokens offer a favorable parameter/performance tradeoff against dense embeddings.

Presentation and limitations: The architecture diagram and task-specific descriptions make the overall pipeline understandable. Appendix A provides losses, learning rates, hardware, and training datasets. Appendix C appropriately acknowledges weaknesses on dynamic scenes, driving environments, and very large view collections. No material ethical concern is apparent from the described work.
weaknesses: Soundness of the central prior-guidance contribution: Pow3R is explicitly identified as supporting similar geometric priors but is never evaluated. The manuscript also lacks a controlled comparison against a VGGT-based model trained with the same additional data and compute. Consequently, the experiments establish that WorldMirror benefits from supplied information, but do not adequately establish the advantage of the proposed prompting framework over existing prior-aware approaches or isolate it from additional training.

The scope of 'any-prior' prompting is insufficiently validated. Training randomly disables entire modalities, while the evaluations do not test partial per-view availability, sparse depth, noisy poses, calibration errors, or conflicting priors. The provenance and preprocessing of evaluation priors are not sufficiently specified. These omissions matter because the introduction motivates real sensor measurements; improvements with accurate reference geometry do not establish robustness in those settings. Simple back-projection or fusion baselines would also contextualize the gains when depth and camera information are supplied.

The claimed benefit of unified multi-task learning is not isolated. There are no matched single-task versus multi-task experiments, no ablation of dynamic prior injection, and no evaluation of the proposed curriculum. Separate prediction heads do not by themselves ensure geometric consistency, and the manuscript provides no direct consistency measurements between predicted points, depths, cameras, and normals. The GS depth-gradient consistency loss supplies only a limited constraint.

Reproducibility and inference details remain materially incomplete. Section 3.2 specifies ground-truth cameras for constructing Gaussian centers without clearly describing the camera source and coordinate/scale handling during image-only inference. The test-time camera alignment protocol is cited but its optimization budget and contribution to runtime are not specified. Appendix A describes both end-to-end training and a final stage with all parameters except the GS head frozen; the exact stage schedule, dataset sampling weights, epoch definition, and normalization/inverse-normalization procedures are missing. Code and weights are only promised.

There is a substantive geometric error: Sections 1 and 4.2 state that calibrated intrinsics resolve scale ambiguity. Known intrinsics alone cannot determine absolute scene scale from unposed images. Moreover, pose translations and depth priors are normalized, but the manuscript does not explain how their metric scale is preserved, how their normalizations remain mutually consistent, or how predictions recover that scale.

Several conclusions overstate the tables. In Table 1, image-only WorldMirror is worse than π3 on every NRGBD metric; Table 2 shows substantially worse Sintel trajectory errors; and Table 7 shows worse KITTI video depth. Table 6 also does not support the assertion that removing any component degrades performance universally: removing ground-truth cameras slightly improves RealEstate10K PSNR, and several ablations improve LPIPS. These results warrant narrower claims and uncertainty estimates, particularly for small differences.

Evaluation fairness and efficiency need clearer documentation. Table 3 does not specify whether WorldMirror receives one image or multiple views when compared with monocular normal predictors. The paper reports feed-forward times below two seconds in Table 8 without inference hardware, resolution, memory use, or precise timing boundaries. These gaps limit confidence in comparisons and the claimed practical efficiency.

strengths: Significance: A single model accepting optional camera, intrinsics, and depth priors while producing several geometric representations is practically useful. Supporting both reconstruction and Gaussian-based rendering broadens the value of the underlying VGGT framework.

Empirical evidence: The reported improvements are substantial in several settings. Without priors, DTU mean reconstruction accuracy improves from 1.198 for π3 to 1.017 (Table 1), ScanNet mean normal error improves from 16.0 for StableNormal to 13.8 (Table 3), and dense RealEstate10K rendering improves from 19.96 to 25.14 PSNR over AnySplat (Table 4).

Originality: Although the components largely build on existing methods, combining flexible prior conditioning with normal and Gaussian prediction is a useful systems contribution. Table 5 supports compact camera and intrinsics tokens as a parameter-efficient conditioning choice, albeit with mixed individual metric results.

Presentation and limitations: The architecture and modality-specific embeddings are understandable, and the appendix provides losses, learning rates, hardware, and dataset names. The discussion candidly identifies limitations concerning dynamic scenes, driving environments, resolution, and sequence length. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the manuscript.
weaknesses: Soundness—camera use in rendering is insufficiently specified. Section 3.2 constructs Gaussian centers using ground-truth poses and intrinsics, while the paper claims pose-free inference. Section 4.3 discusses replacing ground-truth cameras for both Gaussian positioning and rendering, without clearly separating training from evaluation. The manuscript should explicitly document which cameras are used at each stage and how test-time camera alignment operates. This ambiguity prevents a confident assessment of the central pose-free NVS comparison; it does not by itself establish that evaluation uses privileged inputs.

Soundness—claims about arbitrary available priors exceed the demonstrated setting. Training toggles entire modalities, and the experiments primarily show complete modality combinations. They do not establish behavior with priors available for only some views, sparse depth measurements, noisy calibration, or mutually inconsistent priors, despite the motivation involving real sensors. The provenance and preprocessing of evaluation priors also need clearer documentation. Same-modality improvements should be distinguished from cross-task benefits when the supplied prior already contains the evaluated quantity.

Originality and attribution: Pow3R is explicitly identified as an existing reconstruction method accepting additional modalities, but there is no quantitative comparison under a compatible setting. Moreover, there is no matched-data VGGT fine-tuning control, normal-task isolation, or curriculum/prior-dropout ablation. Consequently, the experiments do not establish how much improvement comes from the proposed mechanisms versus additional training and data.

Soundness—geometric consistency and scale claims are overstated. Independent prediction heads sharing a backbone do not ensure mutually consistent point maps, depths, cameras, normals, and Gaussians. Equation 11 supplies a limited depth-gradient constraint, but no quantitative cross-output consistency evaluation is provided. The repeated statement that calibrated intrinsics resolve scale ambiguity is also incorrect in general: global scene scale remains ambiguous without a metric reference. How independently normalized depth and camera translations preserve a common scale is insufficiently explained.

Reproducibility: Appendix A.2 describes both a two-phase schedule and additional curriculum stages without specifying their durations, dataset sampling proportions, or resolution schedule. Depth normalization, pose coordinate conventions, Gaussian voxelization/pruning, evaluation resolutions, and surface-normal input view counts are incompletely specified. The normal view-count omission matters when comparing against monocular methods. Code and weights are only promised, so these details remain necessary for independent reproduction.

Presentation and interpretation: Several conclusions are broader than the tables support. π3 is substantially stronger on NRGBD reconstruction, Sintel camera estimation, and KITTI video depth. Table 6 does not show uniform degradation when components are removed: omitting ground-truth cameras slightly improves RealEstate10K PSNR, and omitting the GS DPT improves VR-NeRF LPIPS. Its full-model results also differ from Table 4 without explanation. These discrepancies, together with the unresolved evaluation details, outweigh the otherwise promising breadth and reported gains.

strengths: Significance: A single model supporting optional camera, intrinsics, and depth priors while predicting geometry, normals, and 3D Gaussians is practically useful. The contribution extends beyond improving one benchmark.

Empirical evidence: Novel-view synthesis gains are substantial. In Table 4, image-only WorldMirror improves over AnySplat from 19.96 to 25.14 PSNR on 32-view RealEstate10K and from 18.40 to 21.25 on 64-view DL3DV, with corresponding SSIM and LPIPS improvements. Tables 1–3 also establish competitive geometry and normal predictions.

Originality: Although the components build on existing architectures, their integration into a flexible multi-output reconstruction system is a meaningful contribution. Table 5 provides useful evidence that compact camera tokens can outperform denser conditioning with fewer additional parameters.

Presentation and transparency: The architecture is generally easy to follow, and the appendix supplies losses, training datasets, learning rates, and prior-dropout probabilities. The limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges weaknesses on dynamic scenes, driving environments, and large view counts. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the manuscript.
weaknesses: Soundness of the central prior-prompting claim: Pow3R is acknowledged as prior work using camera and scene priors but is not evaluated, even in a compatible sparse-view setting. Comparisons primarily show improvement over WorldMirror without priors rather than establish an advantage over existing prior-aware methods. There are also no quantitative tests of noisy, sparse, conflicting, or partially available per-view priors, limiting support for the advertised flexibility in realistic sensor settings.

Novel-view synthesis protocol needs clarification: Section 3.2 explicitly uses ground-truth cameras to construct Gaussian centers, whereas the method is advertised as pose-free. Table 6 suggests this concerns training, but the transition to predicted cameras at inference is not specified clearly. Test-time camera alignment is referenced without sufficient detail about optimization or access to target observations. These omissions prevent confident interpretation of the strongest results; they do not establish that ground-truth cameras were improperly used at test time.

The causal claims about unified learning are insufficiently supported. WorldMirror adds datasets, training stages, normal supervision, and a Gaussian head to pretrained VGGT, without matched-data ablations separating their effects. Neither the proposed curriculum nor dynamic prior injection is ablated. Moreover, Appendix A.2 freezes the backbone during Gaussian-head training, qualifying the repeated claims of end-to-end joint optimization and mutual benefits across all tasks.

Geometric claims require correction or validation. Known intrinsics alone do not resolve global metric scale ambiguity. Independently normalizing pose translations and depth also requires an explicit explanation of their common coordinate system and scale recovery. Shared representations and separate output losses do not by themselves ensure the claimed consistency among point maps, cameras, depth, and normals; direct consistency measurements are absent.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful appendix details. Dataset sampling proportions, precise training-stage boundaries, evaluation resolutions, depth alignment conventions, and inference hardware are insufficiently specified. DL3DV appears in both training and the 'zero-shot' evaluation, so held-out-scene generalization should be distinguished from unseen-dataset generalization. Code and weights are promised but unavailable in the submission.

Claims sometimes exceed the reported evidence. Image-only WorldMirror trails π3 on NRGBD reconstruction, Sintel camera estimation, and several depth metrics. Table 6 does not show degradation in every metric when each component is removed. These results support a strong, versatile system, but not uniformly superior performance or the necessity of every proposed component. The unresolved protocol and attribution issues outweigh the paper's substantial merits in its current form.

strengths: Significance: Combining optional camera, intrinsics, and depth inputs with geometry, normals, and Gaussian prediction is a useful contribution. A single model supporting these configurations could simplify practical reconstruction pipelines.

Soundness: The evaluation covers numerous datasets and tasks, with substantial improvements in several settings. Table 3 reports ScanNet mean normal error of 13.8° versus 16.0° for StableNormal; Table 9 reports RealEstate10K 32-view PSNR of 25.14 versus 19.96 for AnySplat without priors.

The ablations provide meaningful support for individual design choices. Table 13 favors sequential over joint training under matched training steps, Table 14 examines prior dropout, and Table 15 supports additive depth conditioning as an efficient alternative to concatenation.

Presentation and reproducibility: The architecture is generally understandable, and the appendix supplies losses, learning rates, training datasets, computational costs, and additional evaluations. The discussion appropriately acknowledges dynamic-scene, driving-domain, resolution, and memory limitations. The impact statement addresses relevant privacy and misuse concerns; no material ethical violation is evident.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim that prior injection universally improves all predictions is contradicted by reported results. In Table 1, pose conditioning worsens DTU mean completeness from 1.780 to 1.847. In Table 12, even clean depth worsens 7-Scenes accuracy/completeness from 0.044/0.050 to 0.058/0.060. Figure 7 evaluates geometric quantities but does not establish universal benefits for normals and rendering. The conclusions should distinguish frequent improvements from universal gains.

Experimental consistency: Several unexplained differences make the prior-conditioning evidence difficult to interpret. Clean-depth 7-Scenes results are 0.038/0.039 in Table 1 but 0.058/0.060 in Table 12, while no-prior DTU completeness changes from 1.780 to 1.486. The manuscript should identify any checkpoint, sampling, alignment, or evaluation differences before these tables can support a coherent account of robustness.

Reproducibility: Important evaluation details remain insufficiently specified. DL3DV appears in both training and evaluation, but the held-out scene partition is not documented. The pose-free NVS protocol needs an explicit description of inference-time Gaussian placement, alignment between predicted and target cameras, and the parameters and budget used by the pose optimization marked in Table 4. These details matter because Sections 3.2 and A.1 describe Gaussian construction and supervision using ground-truth cameras.

Originality and causal evidence: The contribution primarily integrates VGGT, modality embeddings, additional DPT heads, and established Gaussian prediction components. That integration is useful, but the stronger claim of mutually reinforcing input flexibility and multi-task learning lacks controlled evidence. In particular, there is no matched-data comparison isolating the effect of adding normals or the effect of multi-task training on prior utilization. Freezing the geometry backbone during Gaussian training also limits what can be inferred about reciprocal geometry–appearance benefits.

Significance and presentation: State-of-the-art claims exceed the demonstrated results. π3 remains stronger on NRGBD reconstruction and Sintel camera estimation, and AnySplat has better LPIPS at 24 and 64 views in Table 4. KITTI video depth also trails π3 substantially. These outcomes do not negate the model's usefulness, but they support a versatile, competitive system rather than uniform superiority. Overall, the practical merits are clear, but the evaluation ambiguities and unsupported central generalizations warrant revision before acceptance.

strengths: Significance: Combining optional camera, intrinsics, and depth inputs with five geometric and rendering outputs is practically useful. The contribution is broader than a single benchmark improvement, even though its components build substantially on existing methods.

Empirical merits: The image-only model improves over VGGT across the point-reconstruction benchmarks in Table 1. Surface-normal results are strong, including reducing ScanNet mean angular error from StableNormal’s 16.0 to 13.8 degrees. Table 9 also reports substantial novel-view synthesis gains over AnySplat.

Soundness: The appendix provides meaningful ablations of sequential versus joint training, prior dropout, depth-token fusion, and normalization. Table 13 supports the practical benefit of separating geometry training from Gaussian-head training. Evaluation also covers noisy priors and substantially more views than used during training.

Presentation, reproducibility, and ethics: The architecture is generally understandable, and the appendix supplies losses, learning rates, training datasets, hardware, memory, and latency measurements. The limitations appropriately acknowledge dynamic-scene and scaling weaknesses; the impact statement recognizes privacy, misrepresentation, and bias concerns. No material ethical violation is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—central claims exceed the evidence: Priors do not universally improve predictions. In Table 1, pose conditioning worsens DTU mean completeness from 1.780 to 1.847. In Table 12, even clean depth worsens 7-Scenes accuracy/completeness from 0.044/0.050 to 0.058/0.060. Table 9 also contains a small SSIM regression with pose conditioning. These results support useful but conditional benefits, rather than the universal gains repeatedly claimed in the abstract and conclusion.

Soundness—mutual task benefits are not established: Improvements over separately trained models do not isolate the effect of multi-task learning from training data, initialization, or additional fine-tuning. The backbone is frozen during Gaussian-head training, so that stage cannot improve the geometry heads. Table 13 supports sequential optimization, but does not establish that input flexibility and multi-task prediction are mutually reinforcing. A matched-data VGGT fine-tuning baseline and controlled task-removal experiments are needed to substantiate that interpretation.

Reproducibility—important experimental inconsistencies remain unexplained: Table 1 reports clean-depth 7-Scenes accuracy/completeness of 0.038/0.039, whereas Table 12 reports 0.058/0.060. Their no-prior DTU completeness values also differ substantially, at 1.780 versus 1.486. Different checkpoints or protocols could explain this, but are not identified. The manuscript should reconcile these results and specify the model and evaluation configuration for each ablation.

Method and evaluation clarity: Depth normalization to [0,1] lacks an exact definition and handling of invalid values or cross-view scale. The Gaussian construction description uses ground-truth cameras, but does not clearly explain the corresponding pose-free inference procedure and its scale conventions. Appendix B.2 references test-time camera alignment without detailing what is optimized or its cost, making the relationship between reported rendering quality and feed-forward deployment insufficiently explicit.

Originality and comparative support: Token conditioning, VGGT-based prediction, and an AnySplat-style Gaussian pipeline form a plausible integration, but the manuscript provides limited evidence of a distinct new principle. Figure 5 compares relevant prior-aware methods, yet aggregates reconstruction errors across datasets without per-dataset results, obscuring where the advantage arises. Broad state-of-the-art language also overlooks clear exceptions: π3 is stronger on NRGBD reconstruction and Sintel poses, and AnySplat has better LPIPS at 24 and 64 views in Table 4. Overall, the practical merits are substantial, but the central interpretations and reproducibility gaps require revision before acceptance.

strengths: Significance: A single feed-forward model accepting optional geometric priors and producing geometry, normals, and 3D Gaussians is practically useful. The contribution extends beyond adding outputs: users can exploit available calibration or depth without switching models.

Soundness: Broad experiments support competitive reconstruction and meaningful improvements in normal estimation and rendering. Table 3 reduces ScanNet mean normal error from 16.0° for StableNormal to 13.8°. Table 9 improves RealEstate10K 32-view PSNR from AnySplat’s 19.96 to 25.14 without priors.

Originality: The novelty is primarily a useful integration of established components, supported by design experiments. Compact camera tokens, additive depth conditioning, and sequential geometry/appearance training form a coherent system. Table 13 supports decoupling: NRGBD accuracy improves from 0.084 with joint training to 0.041.

Presentation and reproducibility: The architecture is understandable, and the supplement provides losses, training datasets, learning rates, loss weights, compute costs, evaluation sample counts, and additional ablations. The dropout, noisy-prior, and memory studies substantially strengthen the submission.

Limitations and ethics: The paper appropriately acknowledges difficulties with dynamic scenes, driving environments, and large inputs. Its impact statement identifies relevant privacy, misrepresentation, and bias concerns; no material ethical violation is evident.
weaknesses: Soundness of the strongest claims: 'Universal' improvement across tasks is not established. Table 1 shows camera-pose prompting worsening DTU mean completeness from 1.780 to 1.847, and Table 9 shows slightly worse DL3DV dense-view SSIM with pose prompting. Table 12 even reports clean depth worsening 7-Scenes accuracy from 0.044 to 0.058. Quantitative prior-conditioned normal results are absent. The defensible claim is broad, configuration-dependent benefit.

Experimental consistency: Clean-depth results differ substantially between Table 1 (7-Scenes accuracy/completeness 0.038/0.039) and Table 12 (0.058/0.060), with the latter approximately reproduced in Tables 15–16. The manuscript does not explain a protocol or checkpoint difference. This matters because the discrepancy reverses whether depth prompting helps. Table 8’s sub-two-second feed-forward timing also needs reconciliation with Table 19’s roughly eight seconds at 64 views.

Causal evidence and originality: Improvements do not isolate the proposed synergy between flexible inputs and multi-task learning. The system inherits VGGT initialization, uses extensive training data, and freezes geometry while training the Gaussian head. Table 13 supports sequential over joint optimization, but does not demonstrate mutual task benefits. Matched-data task-removal controls, especially for the normal head, would better distinguish architectural benefits from additional training and supervision.

Reproducibility: Important implementation details remain unclear: whether depth normalization is per image or per scene, how invalid or partially available priors are encoded, and how normalized camera translations and depth share a coordinate scale. The ground-truth-camera training description also needs an explicit inference procedure for constructing Gaussians without camera priors. Dataset mixing proportions, exact sampled evaluation scenes, and uncertainty estimates would improve reproducibility.

Presentation and scope: State-of-the-art claims should reflect mixed results. π3 is substantially better on NRGBD reconstruction, Sintel pose estimation, and KITTI video depth; AnySplat has better LPIPS at 24 and 64 views in Table 4. Calibrated intrinsics alone do not resolve global metric-scale ambiguity, contrary to Section 5.2. These overstatements reduce confidence in the interpretation, although the narrower empirical contribution remains useful and supports weak acceptance.
